deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files from an SSD
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files on an internal SSD are usually gone for good because of TRIM. Learn what to do right now and what small chance remains.
deleted.summary: Modern SSDs use a feature called TRIM: the computer tells the drive which space is free, and the drive treats it as blank, usually right away, then erases it in the background. That means files deleted from an internal SSD are often gone within seconds to hours. Recovery mainly works when TRIM did not run, which is uncommon on Windows and Mac internal drives.
deleted.riskNote: Scanning is safe if you save results elsewhere, but while the SSD keeps running, the system can write new files or send more TRIM commands that erase what is left.
stopFirst: Shut the computer down now. Do not keep browsing or saving files on the SSD.
Do not install recovery software onto the SSD you are trying to recover from.
Do not run a disk cleanup, optimizer or 'trim' tool.

steps.title: Power off right away
steps.detail: The sooner the SSD stops running, the less time it has to erase deleted data in the background. If it is your only drive, shut down instead of just logging out.

steps.title: Check easy backups first
steps.detail: Look in the Recycle Bin or Trash, File History, Time Machine, OneDrive, iCloud or Google Drive. These work far better than recovery software on an SSD.

steps.title: Use a different computer
steps.detail: Connect the SSD to another computer with a USB adapter or dock, or boot from a USB stick with Linux. Do not boot from the SSD itself.

steps.title: Make an image if you can
steps.detail: An image is a full copy of the drive saved to another disk. Use ddrescue to copy the SSD to a drive at least as large, then work only on the copy. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Scan the image with PhotoRec
steps.detail: PhotoRec searches for file contents instead of file names. Save everything it finds to a different drive than the one you are scanning.

steps.title: Try TestDisk for recent deletions
steps.detail: TestDisk can sometimes list deleted files with their original names. It is worth a try, but expect many results to be empty or damaged.

steps.title: Check what you got back
steps.detail: Open a sample of the recovered files. Files that open but are all zeros or blank mean the data was already erased.

deleted.callPro: If the files are extremely valuable, stop after powering off and ask a reputable professional whether anything is still recoverable, since DIY scanning cannot undo TRIM.

faq.q: What is TRIM and why does it matter?
faq.a: TRIM is a message from your operating system telling the SSD which blocks are free. The SSD then erases them, so deleted files really disappear.

faq.q: Are deleted files ever recoverable from an SSD?
faq.a: Sometimes. Results vary with the drive, operating system and settings, and external USB SSDs or older setups may not run TRIM. Treat it as a long shot.

faq.q: Does recovery software work better on an SSD than a hard drive?
faq.a: No, usually worse. A hard drive keeps deleted data until it is overwritten, but an SSD often wipes it on purpose.

formatted.title: Recover Data from a Formatted SSD
formatted.metaDescription: A formatted SSD often loses its data to TRIM within moments. Learn what to do first and when recovery with TestDisk or PhotoRec has a chance.
formatted.summary: Formatting an SSD, especially a full format or a reinstall of the operating system, commonly triggers TRIM, which erases the old data. Quick formats on internal SSDs are usually not recoverable. External or older setups that skip TRIM may still hold data.
formatted.riskNote: Reinstalling Windows or writing new files on the SSD speeds up permanent loss, so careless steps can end any chance of recovery.
stopFirst: Do not copy new files to the SSD or reinstall the operating system on it.
Do not install recovery software on the formatted SSD.
Do not format it again, even if a prompt suggests it.

steps.title: Power down
steps.detail: Turn the computer off. SSDs keep cleaning up in the background while they are powered, which can erase what is left.

steps.title: Move the SSD to another computer
steps.detail: Use a USB adapter or dock, or boot the same computer from a USB Linux stick. Never boot from the formatted SSD.

steps.title: Check for a full or quick format
steps.detail: Think back to what happened. A quick format only clears the index, but on an SSD the data may still be trimmed. A reinstall or full format is almost always final.

steps.title: Image the SSD
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to copy the whole drive to a disk at least as large, then try recovery on the copy as many times as you need. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Look for the lost partition
steps.detail: Run TestDisk on the image. If the old partition is found, you may be able to browse and copy the files.

steps.title: Scan by file type
steps.detail: If TestDisk finds nothing, run PhotoRec on the image. It will recover whatever file contents still exist, without folder names.

steps.title: Save results elsewhere
steps.detail: Write recovered files to a separate drive and open some to confirm they work.

formatted.callPro: If the data is irreplaceable and TestDisk and PhotoRec find nothing, a professional is your only remaining option, though success on a trimmed SSD is unlikely.

faq.q: Will a quick format on an SSD wipe my files?
faq.a: Often yes. The format itself keeps data, but TRIM usually follows and erases it. Odds are better on external SSDs or older systems without TRIM.

faq.q: Can a professional get trimmed data back?
faq.a: Usually not. Once TRIM has run, the SSD reports that space as blank, and a lab mostly helps when the SSD itself has failed.

not-detected.title: SSD Not Detected or Not Showing Up
not-detected.metaDescription: An SSD that does not appear or shows a wrong name and size may have failed firmware. Learn safe checks and when to stop and call a professional.
not-detected.summary: If your computer cannot see the SSD, the cause could be a loose cable, a bad port, or a failed controller. A drive that appears with a strange name or tiny size, such as 'SATAFIRM S11', has a firmware or controller failure and is not a home repair.
not-detected.riskNote: Simple cable and port checks are safe, but repeated power cycling or firmware tools can permanently damage a failing controller.
stopFirst: Do not run firmware flashing tools or 'repair' utilities you found online.
Do not keep power cycling the drive hoping it comes back.
Do not open the drive or use heat or cold on it.

steps.title: Check the basics
steps.detail: With the computer off and unplugged, reseat the SATA or M.2 connection, then try another cable, port or enclosure. Test with a second computer if possible.

steps.title: Look in BIOS and Disk Management
steps.detail: See if the SSD appears in the BIOS or UEFI setup. In Windows, check Disk Management or Disk Utility on a Mac. It might be present but missing a drive letter.

steps.title: Read the name and size
steps.detail: If the drive shows as an odd name like SATAFIRM S11, or as a few megabytes, the controller or firmware has failed. Stop here.

steps.title: Check its health
steps.detail: If it does appear, use smartmontools or CrystalDiskInfo to view health data. Warnings such as low spare blocks or media errors mean the drive is failing.

steps.title: Image immediately if it works
steps.detail: A drive that appears only some of the time may stop for good. Copy it right away with ddrescue to another disk. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Use TestDisk to find lost partitions on the image, then PhotoRec for file contents if needed.

not-detected.callPro: If the SSD never appears or shows the wrong name or size, stop and consult a professional, because many SSDs encrypt data inside the controller and only a specialist can work around a dead one.

faq.q: Why does my SSD show up as SATAFIRM S11?
faq.a: That is a known failure mode where the controller cannot load its firmware and uses a basic safe mode name. Your data is not accessible with normal tools.

faq.q: Can I swap the circuit board to fix an SSD?
faq.a: No, because SSD controllers are tied to the data, often with built-in encryption. Even on hard drives a board swap needs the ROM chip moved, which is lab work.

no-power.title: SSD Dead or Won't Power On
no-power.metaDescription: A dead SSD with no activity or detection usually has a power or controller fault. See what safe checks to try before involving a professional.
no-power.summary: A dead SSD may be fine and the problem lies in the cable, port, adapter or power supply. If those check out, the controller or a power component on the SSD may have failed. SSDs have no moving parts, so there is nothing to listen for.
no-power.riskNote: Checking cables is safe, but repeatedly applying power to a drive with a short circuit can damage it more.
stopFirst: Do not keep plugging it in if you smell burning or see scorch marks.
Do not try to repair the circuit board yourself.
Do not keep power cycling it again and again hoping it comes back.

steps.title: Check for physical damage
steps.detail: Look for burn marks, a cracked board or bent connector pins. If you see damage, stop.

steps.title: Rule out the computer
steps.detail: Try a different cable, port, adapter or computer. Many 'dead' SSDs are really bad USB enclosures or cables.

steps.title: Test in another way
steps.detail: For M.2 drives, try a different slot or a USB-NVMe enclosure. For SATA, try another power cable.

steps.title: Wait before retrying
steps.detail: Some drives need a few minutes on power to recover after a sudden power loss. Do this once: leave it powered in a BIOS screen, not a running operating system, for about 10 minutes, and unplug it if it gets hot.

steps.title: Image if it responds
steps.detail: If the drive reappears, copy it with ddrescue to another disk before doing anything else. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the copy
steps.detail: Run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image, saving results to a different drive.

no-power.callPro: If the SSD is still not detected on a known-good cable and computer, the controller has likely failed and only a professional can attempt recovery.

faq.q: How can I tell if my SSD is dead or just the cable?
faq.a: Test it on a different cable, port and computer. If it fails everywhere, the drive itself is the problem.

faq.q: Does a dead SSD mean my data is gone?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but because many SSDs encrypt data and tie it to the controller, recovery is harder than with hard drives.

liquid-fire.title: SSD Damaged by Water, Fire or Impact
liquid-fire.metaDescription: Water, fire or heat damage to an SSD needs careful handling. Learn what not to do, including never powering it on, and when to call a professional.
liquid-fire.summary: Liquid, smoke, heat or a hard impact can short out an SSD or crack its memory chips. Powering it on can finish the damage. Your best chance is to keep it off and let a specialist look at it.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Powering on or heat-drying a damaged SSD can short the board and destroy data that was otherwise intact.
stopFirst: Do not plug the SSD in or power on the device it is in.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven, rice or any heat.
Do not shake it, clean the contacts or open it.

steps.title: Disconnect power
steps.detail: If the SSD is in a laptop, unplug the charger, and remove the battery and SSD only if they come out easily. If the battery is swollen, hot or smoking, do not handle it; move away and call the fire service.

steps.title: Keep it still and dry
steps.detail: Place the drive in a clean, dry, anti-static bag or container. Do not rinse or wipe it, whatever the liquid was.

steps.title: Note what happened
steps.detail: Write down the kind of liquid or the heat exposure. This helps any specialist decide on the safest approach.

steps.title: Check for backups
steps.detail: While you wait, look for cloud backups, other copies and old backup drives. These may save the day.

steps.title: Decide on professional help
steps.detail: The only safe options are to leave it alone or send it to a lab that handles liquid damage. Ask about their no-fix, no-fee policy first.

liquid-fire.callPro: Contact a professional before attempting any power-on, since damaged SSDs are very fragile and DIY steps usually reduce the chance of recovery.

faq.q: Can I dry out a wet SSD and try it?
faq.a: No. Even after it looks dry, residue on the board can cause shorts. Do not use heat or rice.

faq.q: Is a burned SSD always unrecoverable?
faq.a: Not always. If the memory chips are intact, a specialist may be able to repair the board so the original controller can read them, but results vary a lot.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted or RAW SSD Safely
corrupted.metaDescription: SSD shows RAW, asks to format, or has unreadable files? Make an image first, then use TestDisk and PhotoRec. Do not format or run chkdsk yet.
corrupted.summary: Corruption means the drive's file index or partition information is damaged, even though the data may still be there. Sometimes it is a software issue, and sometimes the SSD is starting to fail. Work from a copy to avoid making it worse.
corrupted.riskNote: Letting Windows format or repair the drive, or running chkdsk, can overwrite the index information you need to recover your files.
stopFirst: Do not click Format when the system says the drive must be formatted.
Do not run chkdsk or any 'repair' prompt before making a copy.
Do not install recovery software onto the problem SSD.

steps.title: Stop and check health
steps.detail: Use smartmontools or CrystalDiskInfo to look at the drive's health. Many errors or low remaining life suggest the SSD is failing.

steps.title: Back up what is readable
steps.detail: If you can open the drive, copy important files to another disk right now.

steps.title: Image the drive
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to copy the SSD to a drive at least as large, and keep its map file so the copy can resume if the SSD disconnects. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Look for the partition
steps.detail: Open the image in TestDisk and run an Analyse. It can often find and restore a lost partition or repair the boot sector.

steps.title: Copy files out
steps.detail: If TestDisk shows your folders, copy the files to a different drive. Do not write the repair back to the original yet.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec as a backup plan
steps.detail: If the folders cannot be found, PhotoRec can pull files by type from the image, though names will be lost.

steps.title: Repair only at the end
steps.detail: After everything is safely copied, you can reformat the SSD or run Windows repair tools. If the health check showed errors, replace the SSD instead of trusting it again.

corrupted.callPro: If the SSD disconnects repeatedly, reports very few usable blocks, or the imaging stalls, stop and get professional help.

faq.q: Why does my SSD say it needs to be formatted?
faq.a: The file system information is damaged or unreadable. Your files may still exist, so do not format.

faq.q: Is it safe to run chkdsk on an SSD?
faq.a: Not before you have a copy. Chkdsk changes the drive and can delete data it cannot fix.

encrypted.title: Recover Data from an Encrypted SSD
encrypted.metaDescription: Encrypted SSDs need the password or recovery key. Find BitLocker, FileVault or VeraCrypt keys and learn why brute force is not a real option.
encrypted.summary: If your SSD is protected with BitLocker, FileVault, VeraCrypt or built-in hardware encryption, the data is scrambled without the key. Without the password or recovery key, recovery is not realistically possible. The good news is that keys are often stored somewhere you can find.
encrypted.riskNote: Wrong attempts, resets, or erasing the drive's encryption can make the data permanently unreadable.
stopFirst: Do not reset, secure erase or 'crypto erase' the SSD.
Do not reinstall the operating system over the encrypted drive.
Do not trust any site or service that promises to crack encryption.

steps.title: Identify the encryption type
steps.detail: Look for BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on Mac, VeraCrypt volumes, or a hardware password set in the BIOS or drive utility.

steps.title: Find the recovery key
steps.detail: For BitLocker, sign in at your Microsoft account's recovery key page or check work or school accounts, printouts and USB keys. For FileVault, check iCloud or the key you saved; on newer Macs the SSD is built in and can only be unlocked in that Mac.

steps.title: Check password managers
steps.detail: Search your password manager, notes, emails and old documents for the password or key.

steps.title: Unlock on a working system
steps.detail: Connect the SSD to a computer running the same type of encryption and unlock it normally with the key. Copy the files to another drive.

steps.title: Image before risky actions
steps.detail: Only if you have the key and the drive is also failing: image it with ddrescue first. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data. A drive locked with a hardware password must be unlocked before it can be copied.

steps.title: Recover from the unlocked copy
steps.detail: Once unlocked, use TestDisk or PhotoRec on the unlocked volume if files are missing.

encrypted.callPro: If the SSD controller fails on a hardware-encrypted drive, or you are locked out with no key, only a professional can say whether anything is possible, and often the answer is no.

faq.q: Can encrypted data be recovered without the key?
faq.a: In practice, no. Modern encryption with a strong password cannot realistically be guessed or bypassed, so beware of anyone claiming to do so.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker recovery key?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, a work or school account, a printout, or a file saved to a USB stick.
